title: The Seeker's Question
on_slide_text: The austere sage Valmiki, steeped in Vedic study, asks Narada, knower of words: who lives now, filled with virtue, prowess, duty, gratitude, truth, firm vows, and welfare for all beings, controlled, pleasing, malice-free, feared even by gods in battle?
rationale: Opens on Valmiki's hook question to Narada, establishing the criterion quest that frames the entire Ramayana.

title: Measure Before Hero
question: Why does Valmiki ask Narada who the complete man is at this time before beginning the tale, instead of simply starting Rama's story?
answer: Valmiki forges the criterion before seeking the person — listing gratitude, truth, firmness in vow and care for subjects' happiness — because without a standard a story stays mere entertainment. Modern minds repeat the mistake, hunting heroes without asking what human to become. Narada's yes proves the ideal can be history, not sky, so we should write three life-measures and test every inspiring story against them.
on_slide_text: Why forge the measure before telling the tale? Because without a standard of gratitude, truth, and care for subjects, story stays entertainment; Valmiki first builds the criterion, then finds the man, teaching us to write our three life-measures before admiring any hero.
rationale: Pauses right after the hook to unpack why method precedes story, drawn from the first reflection.

title: Rama Named
on_slide_text: Narada answers with delight: in Ikshvaku's line is born Rama, controlled in soul, great in prowess, radiant, patient, restrained, wise, moral, sweet-spoken, graceful, foe-destroying, ever engaged in his subjects' good, increasing Kausalya's joy.
rationale: Delivers Narada's delighted answer naming Rama, the central beat that the ideal exists.

title: Body Certifies Soul
on_slide_text: Broad shoulders, knee-long arms, conch neck, broad chest, cool hue, large eyes, auspicious marks, firm promise, pure, humble, self-knowing, skilled archer. Like Prajapati he protects, grave like sea, patient like Himalaya, strong like Vishnu, lovely like moon, fiery in anger, earth in forgiveness, generous like Kubera, true like Dharma.
rationale: Presents the full portrait beat where physical marks and cosmic similes together certify moral stature.

title: Flesh Shows Virtue
question: Why does Narada string bodily marks like a conch-like neck and knee-long arms in the same garland as moral virtues like truth, forgiveness and compassion?
answer: This is not body-worship but philosophy where body is character's certificate — broad chest means readiness to carry responsibility, large eyes practice equal vision, cool hue victory over agitation, and modern psychology agrees in shoulder tension and jaw clench. Virtues descend into daily flesh, so once a day observe shoulders, breath and eyes without mirror to ask which quality the body reveals.
on_slide_text: Why braid conch neck and knee-long arms with truth and forgiveness? Because body certifies character: broad chest to carry duty, large eyes for equal vision, cool hue beyond agitation, teaching us to read today's shoulders, breath, and gaze for the virtue they reveal.
rationale: Reflects on the portrait just shown, explaining why flesh and virtue belong in one garland.

title: Two Boons Exile
on_slide_text: King Dasharatha lovingly prepares to crown virtuous Rama heir for his people's good, when Queen Kaikeyi claims two old boons: forest exile for Rama and coronation for Bharata. Bound by promise-duty, the king sends his dear son, and Rama obeys to honor Kaikeyi.
rationale: Covers the turning beat where coronation hope flips to exile by boons and duty.

title: Ganga to Chitrakuta
on_slide_text: On exile's eve humble Lakshmana joins like brother-love, and Janaka's Sita follows like Rohini follows moon, dear as life. Father and citizens trail behind. At Sringaverapura's Ganga bank Rama meets good Nishada Guha and sends the charioteer back.
rationale: Follows the forest departure beat with Lakshmana, Sita, Guha and farewell to Ayodhya.

title: Sandals of Trust
on_slide_text: Guided by Bharadwaja, they build a lovely Chitrakuta dwelling and live joyfully like gods, while grieving Dasharatha weeps to heaven. Pressed by Vashishtha's Brahmanas, Bharata refuses the throne, seeks Rama in forest, receives sandals, and rules waiting from Nandigrama.
rationale: Completes the Ayodhya aftermath with death, refusal, sandals and waiting rule at Nandigrama.

title: Power as Trust
question: Why does Rama accept an unjust exile to protect Dasharatha's word, and why does Bharata, offered an unsought kingdom, leave with the sandals for Nandigrama?
answer: The issue is trust, not obedience — if the king's boon broke, the institution of the word would break, so Rama sacrifices right to save collective faith, while Bharata refuses a maneuvered throne to avoid breaking order twice. Both treat power as trust, not prasad, one ripening in forest and one waiting in village, against modern hunger for power, so pause a day before accepting unearned gain to ask if it strengthens trust.
on_slide_text: Why does Rama accept unjust exile and Bharata refuse a free throne? Because power is trust, not prize: Rama saves the king's word to keep collective faith, Bharata rejects maneuvered gain to heal order, urging us to pause a day before accepting unearned credit or post.
rationale: Interprets the exile and sandals beats as a shared psychology of trust over power.

title: Vow Against Rakshasas
on_slide_text: Seeing crowds, Rama enters Dandaka, kills deformed Viradha, honors Sharabhanga, Sutikshna, Agastya and his brother. At Agastya's word he takes Indra's bow, inexhaustible arrows, sword and quiver, then vows before fire-glowing sages to destroy Rakshasas in battle.
rationale: Marks entry into Dandaka, arming by Agastya and the vow that launches the forest war.

title: Fourteen Thousand Fall
on_slide_text: In Janasthana, form-changing Shurpanakha is disfigured, and at her cry Khara, Trishira and Dushana rush with followers. Lotus-eyed Rama stands alone and slays them all, fourteen thousand Rakshasas falling in that terrible battle.
rationale: Isolates the Janasthana battle beat where disfigurement triggers mass slaughter.

title: Abduction Grief
on_slide_text: Maddened by kinsmen's death, Ravana seeks Maricha, who warns spare me, make no enmity with the strong. Fate-driven, Ravana ignores him, uses illusion to lure Rama and Lakshmana far, kills Jatayu, abducts Mithila's Sita, leaving Rama weeping in grief.
rationale: Preserves the climactic abduction beat with Maricha's warning, illusion, Jatayu and grief unmerged.

title: Shabari to Friendship
on_slide_text: Sorrowing, Rama cremates Jatayu, slays and burns dreadful Kabandha who rises to heaven bidding seek moral Shabari. Rama honors Shabari, then on Pampa's bank meets Hanuman, and through him makes fire-witnessed friendship with Sugriva, vowing to kill Vali.
rationale: Traces the search chain from funeral rites through Kabandha and Shabari to Hanuman and alliance.

title: Fall of Vali
on_slide_text: To cure Sugriva's fear Rama with his toe flings hill-like Dundubhi's corpse ninety miles, then one arrow pierces seven palms, hill, down to nether world. Convinced, golden Sugriva roars at Kishkindha; with Tara's leave Vali comes, and Rama fells him, granting kingdom to Sugriva.
rationale: Shows proof of strength and the single-arrow fall of Vali that wins Sugriva's kingdom.

title: Periphery Saves Center
question: Why must Ayodhya's prince make a fire-witnessed friendship with forest-dwellers like Sugriva and Hanuman to win over Ravana?
answer: When the center breaks, the periphery saves — palace intrigue exiled Rama, but forest gave search, army and flight, and Hanuman's hundred-yojana leap to the Ashoka grove shows epics win by relationships, not valor alone. The hero wins by joining a different world, for greatness lies in connection, so for any stuck problem seek help from one person outside rank and familiar circle.
on_slide_text: Why must Ayodhya's prince befriend forest monkeys to defeat Ravana? Because when the center breaks, the periphery saves: exile lost a palace but gained search, army, and flight, proving heroes win by joining a different world, so seek help outside rank for any stuck problem.
rationale: Reflects on the forest alliance just formed, framing it as the epic's modern signal.

title: Leap to Ashoka
on_slide_text: Made king, Sugriva sends monkeys all ways for Janaki. On Sampati's word mighty Hanuman leaps hundred-yojana salt sea, finds worried Sita in Ashoka grove, shows token, speaks of friendship, comforts her, smashes gate, slays five generals, ministers' sons and Aksha, then yields to Indrajit's weapon.
rationale: Covers the search climax with leap, discovery, token, comfort and capture.

title: Lanka Burns Ocean Rises
on_slide_text: Freed by grandsire's boon, Hanuman forgives captors, spares only Sita's place, burns all Lanka, returns circling Rama crying truly seen Sita. With Sugriva Rama reaches vast ocean shore, troubles deeps with sun-arrows till ocean lord of rivers appears.
rationale: Links burning of Lanka and glad news to troubling the ocean, bridging search to invasion.

title: Bridge Battle Fire
on_slide_text: On ocean's counsel Nala bridges the sea; Rama crosses to Lanka and kills Ravana in battle. Regaining Sita, shamed Rama speaks harsh words before all; unable to bear it she enters blazing fire, Agni attests her sinlessness, gods rejoice, and Vibhishana receives Lanka's throne.
rationale: Holds the central climax unmerged away: bridge, killing, fire ordeal and new throne.

title: Return and Golden Rule
on_slide_text: Booned, Rama revives monkeys, flies Pushpaka via Bharadwaja's hermitage, sends Hanuman to Bharata, sheds locks at Nandigrama, regains Sita and kingdom, guarding subjects like father. His reign brings health, no widowhood, no famine fear, full grain like golden age, hundred sacrifices, ten thousand and hundred years rule, holy merit to readers.
rationale: Closes the story arc with revival, Pushpaka return, coronation and Ramarajya merit.

title: Love Tested Order Promised
question: Why does Rama speak harsh words before all after winning Sita back, and why does the tale then imagine a Ramarajya with no untimely death or fear?
answer: Here is the double trial of the ideal — public suspicion wounds even private love, Rama pays the price of becoming the man of limits while Sita entering fire declares autonomy. The Ramarajya that follows is not report but vow, a map free from fear, hunger and theft, warning even ideal persons can err so ideal order is needed, so choose proof and dialogue before accusation and make one concrete rule for fearlessness.
on_slide_text: Why harsh words after victory, then a fearless Ramarajya? Because public doubt wounds private love: Rama, bound as ideal king, errs, Sita asserts autonomy in fire, teaching proof before accusation, and calling us to build one fearless rule at home.
rationale: Ends on the sharpest insight, turning fire ordeal and Ramarajya vow into closing moral.
